newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh bid to finance securities faces snags.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh bid to finance securities faces snags.

text.p: A government move to inject fresh funds into Bangladesh's fledgling capital market after a recent scam has hit a snag because the country's biggest commerical bank declined to comply, financial sources said on Tuesday.
They said the government had asked the four, state-owned commercial banks to "save the capital market" by investing directly in equities.
Three of the banks have already invested a total of one billion taka but the Sonali Bank refused, saying it could not play risky game with public money.
The board of directors of the Sonali Bank said expert opinion suggested that "we cannot destroy or play game with deposits of our valued customers knowing that such investment could be bad one."

It cited a survey report by M.A. Baqui Khalily, professor of finance and banking at the Dhaka University, whom the bank hired, as saying that the stock market had to be stable and efficient before one could stake public money.

"Erratic price behaviour and inefficiency in the stock markets through manipulation and information distortions and the use of invisible hands is likely to lead to shallow investment deepening as it will limit wide participation of the investors because of scariness and incomplete information," said the report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.

One bank source told Reuters on Tuesday that the Finance Ministry had asked the state-owned banks to pump in new funds to "save" the capital market after the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) accused major market players of manipulating share prices, causing heavy losses to many investors.

An inquiry instituted by the SEC, the capital market watchdog, had found 36 top dealers and company owners had been invlolved in "fraudulent activities," sending the all-share index of the Dhaka Stcok Exchange (DSE) up above 3,600 points in October-November 1996 and then crashing down to 1,127.09 on Monday.
A Dhaka court subsequently ordered the accused to be arrested but they obtained interim bail from the High Court while restriction imposed on their foreign travels remain.
SEC chairman Dr. Haroonur Rashid said "the government has been watching the situation quite cautiously, and would take more measures to restore confidence of the investors."

Bangladesh's central bank meanwhile announced a package of measures to rejuvenate the capital market, including increased loans for investors from the state-run Investment Corporation of Bangladesh and permission to set up merchant banks.
